selected.name: States conditions under which the claim holds
selected.instruction: Score how explicitly the abstract bounds its own claim: assumptions, regime of validity, and approximation status. 10: the limits are stated in the authors' own voice ('under mild conditions'; 'we give rigorous analysis in a large local region'; 'using recently derived (non-rigorous) risk estimates under a Gaussian universality ansatz'), so a reader can say where the result would stop holding. 5: some scoping language appears but the operative claim is still unconditional. 0: claims are unconditional and intensified, with no regime, no assumption, and no acknowledgement that any condition is needed.
selected.rationale: R02 flags its own non-rigor and its ansatz, R55 restricts its rigorous analysis to a local region, and R01 says 'under mild conditions' - all dense_high_card_low, and all penalized by the same honesty if a criterion bank credits confident, complete claims. In the card-favored direction, R11 promises 'near-optimal efficacy and long-term retention' and R60 reports 'extraordinary capabilities' with no stated condition anywhere.
member_names: States conditions under which the claim holds

selected.name: Controlled isolation of causal contribution
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract describes controlled removals, substitutions, or matched comparisons that isolate why a component matters; score 0 when only the intact system is compared with baselines and no component-level test is stated.
selected.rationale: R20 isolates normalization choices and clean/adversarial data effects, R37 isolates the embedding layer, and R59 systematically deconstructs diffusion-model components.

selected.name: Diagnosis-to-mechanism coherence
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a concrete failure mechanism and the proposed design follows directly from that diagnosis, with the causal chain made explicit; score 0 when motivation, method, and claimed benefit are generic or disconnected.
selected.rationale: R01 links model error to uncertainty-weighted conservatism, while R20 links mixed-domain normalization to separate statistics. R37 similarly connects embedding-layer gradients to a targeted freezing intervention.

selected.name: Uncertainty-aware reasoning
selected.instruction: Score 10 when uncertainty, ambiguity, or competing knowledge sources are explicitly represented, estimated, and used to guide inference, control, or interpretation; score 0 when the abstract assumes a single certain answer despite an identified ambiguity.
selected.rationale: R01 uses epistemic uncertainty to blend estimates, R06 estimates out-of-distribution uncertainty, and R46 operationalizes label uncertainty. R24 also distinguishes competing forms of knowledge reliability.

selected.name: Structure-Matched Inductive Bias
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the architecture encodes the problem’s relevant geometry, dependencies, hierarchy, or symmetry; score 0 when the architecture is generic and imposes no visibly relevant structural bias.
selected.rationale: R12, R41, R57, and R59 build model structure around sensor dynamics, physical discretization, state-goal interactions, or higher-order logic.

selected.name: Enumerated contributions are genuinely separable findings
selected.instruction: Where the abstract enumerates contributions, score whether the items are independent findings or objects that could each stand without the others. 10: the enumerated items are separable - for instance two unrelated properties of the same training regime, one about normalization and one about network capacity, either of which could be published alone. 5: items are distinct but only as parts of one contribution. 0: the enumeration is the step list of a single pipeline (build a dataset, then use it to identify something, then use that to do a thing) or one idea partitioned into several labelled sub-claims. Abstracts that do not enumerate should be scored on whether their claims are separable in the same sense.
selected.rationale: R44 enumerates two genuinely independent findings and R45 reports several distinct measurements of the early training phase; both are dense_high_card_low. Card-favored R13 ('three major technical contributions') and R19 (five named preference aspects) present one pipeline and one taxonomy respectively, cut into numbered pieces - a shape that reads as rich contribution to a bank counting contributions, and as one idea to a reader tracking what is actually separable. R11 uses bold headers for the same effect.
member_names: Enumerated contributions are genuinely separable findings

selected.name: Positions against a specific account and names its gap
selected.instruction: Score whether the abstract engages a particular existing explanation, taxonomy, or standard practice and states exactly what it gets wrong - not merely that prior work is insufficient. 10: the target and the defect are both specific (standard concentration of measure fails to characterize intrinsic robustness because it ignores labels; an existing benign/tempered/catastrophic taxonomy needs refinement and the paper says along which axis; most modern diffusion components turn out to be nonessential for representation learning). 5: prior work is named but its defect is generic. 0: prior work is characterized only as costly, impractical, or limited, with no account of what it claims or why the claim fails.
selected.rationale: R27, R02 and R33 are dense_high_card_low and each argues with a named position rather than a citation cloud. Card-favored R51 and R11 describe prior approaches only by cost and inconvenience ('significant costs', 'redundant capabilities', 'often struggle with rapid updates', 'increasing storage requirements'), which satisfies a 'motivates against prior work' check while conveying no disagreement a reader could adjudicate.
member_names: Positions against a specific account and names its gap

selected.name: Specific technical problem framing vs generic trend-hype opening
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 on the opening motivation of the abstract: a 10 means the first 1-2 sentences state a precise technical gap or question specific to the problem; a 0 means the opening leans on a generic industry-trend claim ('X have shown remarkable Y', 'with the rapid development of Z') that could preface almost any paper in the area.
selected.rationale: R02 opens with 'Agents powered by large language models have shown remarkable abilities in solving complex tasks'; R06 opens with 'With the rapid development of AI-generated content, the future internet may be inundated...'. Contrast R11 and R46, which open directly with the specific technical object under study.
member_names: Specific technical problem framing vs generic trend-hype opening

selected.name: Composable Mechanistic Design
selected.instruction: Score 10 when multiple components have explicit roles and interfaces that jointly resolve a stated failure mode; score 0 when components are merely concatenated without a reasoned interaction.
selected.rationale: R09, R13, and R24 describe mobility-navigation, motif-generation, or flow-composition interactions whose value depends on how parts work together.

selected.name: Headline number interpretable and anchored to stated setting
selected.instruction: Score the principal quantitative claim for interpretability and anchoring. 10: the number carries units or a directly meaningful scale and names the setting in which it was measured (time-of-flight error below 0.33 ns in indoor scenarios; the proportion of energetically favorable poses rises from 30% to 73% on a named docking benchmark). 5: a relative gain over a specific named baseline on a named benchmark. 0: a bare relative superlative over unnamed competitors ('surpasses all other open-source models by a substantial margin', 'significantly outperforms existing methods'), or a single score with no reference point.
selected.rationale: R36 and R53 are dense_high_card_low and both report quantities a domain reader can convert into physical meaning without consulting a leaderboard. Card-favored R60, R11 and R50 report margins over unspecified fields or an isolated F1. A criterion bank asking 'are results quantified?' scores both kinds identically, since both contain numbers; the distinction between an anchored physical quantity and a free-floating margin is precisely what such a check cannot see.
member_names: Headline number interpretable and anchored to stated setting

selected.name: Reproducibility specificity
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract gives concrete reproduction-enabling details—named datasets or tasks, operating regimes, baselines, artifacts, and implementation availability; score 0 when it offers only generic experimental language or a bare code link or promise.
selected.rationale: R02, R11, R28, and R55 identify concrete tasks, regimes, artifacts, or released resources. This distinguishes substantive reproducibility information from checklist-friendly publicity alone.

selected.name: Intervention-backed interpretability
selected.instruction: Score 10 when internal features are probed and then causally manipulated or behaviorally checked through an intervention tied to the task; score 0 when interpretability consists only of visualizations, correlations, or labels applied after the fact.
selected.rationale: R40 probes hidden directions and edits them at inference, while R26 identifies and manipulates personality-related neurons. R09 adds a less direct example by relating learned representations to constituent dynamics.

selected.name: Existence-only proof vs constructive, demonstrated theoretical claim
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 jointly on (a) whether the abstract makes a formal/theoretical claim AND (b) whether that claim is tied to an explicit construction, algorithm, or experiment that instantiates it. A 10 is a precise theoretical claim accompanied by a concrete algorithm, construction, or experiment demonstrating it in practice. A 0 is a purely existential claim ('there exists...', 'we prove the existence of...') with no accompanying construction, algorithm, or empirical demonstration reported in the abstract.
selected.rationale: R19 proves only that certified-robust networks 'exist,' with no construction or experiment reported in the abstract; contrast R14, which derives an explicit optimization algorithm with stated iteration complexity and applies it to a concrete hidden-convexity problem, and R31, which builds and analyzes an explicit minimal function.
member_names: Existence-only proof vs constructive, demonstrated theoretical claim

selected.name: Low packaging density: few coined acronyms, sparse raw statistics
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 inversely with 'packaging density': count coined acronyms/brand names for the method, dataset, and/or benchmark together with the frequency of standalone specific numbers (percentages, counts, sample sizes) not woven into an explanatory sentence. A 10 uses plain descriptive language, at most one simple method name, and numbers only in service of a stated argument. A 0 uses multiple coined acronyms (e.g., separate names for the dataset and the benchmark) plus several free-standing statistics presented as a checklist of achievements.
selected.rationale: R06 (LOKI) reports '18K carefully curated questions across 26 subcategories' and '22 open-source LMMs and 6 closed-source models' as a checklist of scale statistics; R23 coins SELF-PARAM as a nested acronym-of-an-acronym. Contrast R27 and R46, which use no coined branding and almost no free-standing statistics.
member_names: Low packaging density: few coined acronyms, sparse raw statistics

selected.name: Reusable Knowledge Interface
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the learned representation or interface can be reused, updated, composed, or controlled across substantially different tasks; score 0 when it serves only one fixed task with no reuse mechanism.
selected.rationale: R16, R33, R54, and R57 present knowledge fusion, updateable memory, motor primitives, or factorized values as reusable interfaces.

selected.name: Contemporary large-language-model and agent subject-matter vocabulary
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 how saturated the text is with current large-language-model and agent vocabulary: large language models or LLMs, agents, prompts, instruction tuning, alignment or preference optimisation, LoRA, quantised serving of LLMs, multimodal LMMs, named recent chat systems. 0 = none of this vocabulary; 5 = the topic touches it in passing; 10 = the text sits entirely inside that vocabulary. Score only vocabulary saturation. Do NOT judge whether the topic is timely, important, fashionable, crowded or overdone.
selected.rationale: This vocabulary is heavily on the card-high side: R09, R15, R21, R23, R25, R27, R41, R55 and R59 all carry it with card_pct running from .765 to .991, while the dense_high_card_low side is dominated by pre-LLM reinforcement-learning, optimisation and theory vocabulary (R17 card .019, R31 card .018, R42 card .025, R24 card .079, R32 card .138). Terminology vintage records when an item was produced, not what it is worth, and it can shift a text-only model wholesale. Counter-instances exist (R29, R34 and R07 use older vocabulary yet score card-high), which is why this is proposed as a suspected nuisance to be discounted rather than a confirmed effect.
member_names: Contemporary large-language-model and agent subject-matter vocabulary

selected.name: Explicit comparison to named commercial frontier models
selected.instruction: Read the abstract only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract explicitly names specific commercial/proprietary frontier systems as baselines, tools, or comparison points (e.g. 'GPT-4', 'GPT-4o', 'ChatGPT', 'Claude', 'Gemini'). 0 = no such names; 10 = multiple such names are central to the comparison. Do not judge whether beating or using these systems indicates a better paper -- only report how much explicit name-dropping of branded commercial systems is present.
selected.rationale: R33 explicitly beats 'ChatGPT-3.5, Claude Instant, Gemini Pro and Mistral Medium' and R23 uses 'GPT-4/4o' to generate its training data; both are dense_low_card_high (card_pct=0.883, 0.940). Naming and comparing against costly proprietary frontier models requires both being active in the current hype window and having API budget -- an upstream resourcing/timing factor that could genuinely correlate with more thorough work (mixed) but is not itself research quality.
member_names: Counted experimental scale and named comparison systems

selected.name: Abstract length and sentence-count verbosity
selected.instruction: Read the abstract only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how long and elaborated the abstract is, based purely on word count, sentence count, and number of paragraph breaks -- NOT on what claims it makes or how good the work sounds. Score 0 if the abstract is extremely terse (roughly 1-3 short sentences), 5 for a typical single-paragraph abstract of moderate length, and 10 if it is unusually long and multi-paragraph with many clauses. Do not judge whether the length is appropriate, well-used, or a sign of quality -- only report how much length/verbosity is present.
selected.rationale: R13 ('Logic and the 2-Simplicial Transformer') is a two-sentence abstract yet has dense_pct=0.999 (top of dense) but card_pct=0.018 (near-bottom of scorecard); by contrast R34 and R45 are long, multi-clause, multi-paragraph abstracts with card_pct=0.920 and 0.986 respectively. Length is a pure textual surface feature that plausibly drives scorecard aggregation (more text = more surface for criteria to find something to reward) independent of the underlying research's merit.

selected.name: Conversion and formatting artifacts
selected.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much visible text contains line-break hyphenation, TeX commands, spacing anomalies, malformed links, stray markup, or other extraction artifacts. Judge only artifact extent; do not judge whether the presentation is good.
selected.rationale: Text-extraction artifacts can influence a text model independently of the research. R04 contains broken hyphenation and R55 contains a malformed repeated URL.

selected.name: Promotional superlative density
selected.instruction: Score 0-10: how much language such as “first,” “remarkable,” “significant,” “unprecedented,” or “state-of-the-art” appears? Judge only its extent, not whether any claim is good, correct, or important.
selected.rationale: A text model may treat emphatic framing as a shortcut unrelated to research merit. Examples include R03, R11, R18, and R34.

selected.name: Artifact-release and availability boilerplate
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 how much of the text is devoted to statements that code, data, weights, checkpoints, demos or project pages are or will be released or publicly available, including promissory forms such as 'we will release'. 0 = no availability statement anywhere; 5 = one short standard sentence; 10 = several such statements, or a prominent multi-clause release block. Score only the presence and prominence of availability language. Do NOT verify the claim, do NOT judge whether releasing artifacts is good practice, and do NOT judge reproducibility.
selected.rationale: Release boilerplate is concentrated on one side of the disagreement: R06 ('Code is released on our project page', card .980), R13 (card .965), R19 ('Both datasets are publicly available', card .961), R14 (card .947), R47 (card .918), R56 (card .920), R57 (card .926), R59 (card .940) and R21 ('We will release our code', card .784) are all dense_low_card_high, while dense_high_card_low items such as R31, R26 and R42 carry none. The sentence is one clause of costless text and a promissory form costs nothing at all; it fingerprints a group with staff to package artifacts rather than saying anything about the findings. Marked mixed because groups that can package artifacts plausibly also do more careful work.

upstream_parent_all_members: engineering headcount and lab release norms

selected.name: Formal symbolic texture
selected.instruction: Score 0-10: how much the abstract uses equations, Greek symbols, asymptotic notation, formal definitions, or theorem-like language? Judge only the extent, not whether the mathematics is correct or meaningful.
selected.rationale: Formal notation can act as a prestige or technicality cue to a text model while being independent of research merit. Examples include R08, R29, R46, and R54.

selected.name: Coined acronym/brand name in the title
selected.instruction: Read the title and abstract. On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the title coins and foregrounds an invented capitalized acronym or brand name for the proposed method (e.g., a memorable all-caps or CamelCase name standing in for 'our method'). 0 = purely descriptive title with no coined name; 10 = title is dominated by a prominent invented brand/acronym. Do not judge whether the name is a good name or whether branding indicates a better method -- only report how much brand-coinage is present.
selected.rationale: R07 ('LoftQ'), R33 ('WizardMath'), R45 ('LOKI'), and R59 ('InfinityGAN') all coin a prominent brand name in the title and are in the dense_low_card_high subset (card_pct=0.784, 0.883, 0.986, 0.882); this naming convention is an orthographic/marketing habit, not a quality signal.
member_names: Coined acronym/brand name in the title

selected.name: Identity-revealing URLs, handles and organisation-named hosts
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text contains strings that could identify the producing person, group or organisation: personal handles or personal names inside a repository URL, lab or company project-page domains, an organisation name inside a repository path, named institutional hosts. 0 = no URLs, or only neutral ones with no identifying token; 5 = one URL containing a handle or lab name; 10 = several identity-bearing links, or an explicitly organisation-branded host or path. Score only how identity-revealing the visible strings are. Do NOT try to infer or state who the producers actually are, do NOT judge their standing, and do NOT judge whether including links is good.
selected.rationale: De-anonymising strings cluster on the card-high side: R57 links a path containing an organisation name, google-research (card .926); R06 gives a lab project page, ali-design.github.io (card .980); R41 an organisation host, opendatalab.github.io (card .986); R45 a personal page, yanghtr.github.io (card .731); R56 a repository under a full personal name (card .920); R13 and R11 repositories under personal handles (card .965 and .869). Reputation is an unseen upstream factor that can only bias a text-only model through traces like these, which is what makes the visible trace, not the reputation, the scorable thing. Marked mixed because recognisable groups plausibly also produce stronger work. Note R17 carries a bare video link with no organisational token and sits at card .019, so a neutral URL is not the same feature.
member_names: Identity-revealing URLs, handles and organisation-named hosts

selected.name: Importance preamble before any contribution is stated
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 how much of the opening is spent asserting that the problem area matters before anything the work itself did is named. Look for constructions such as 'X is essential/critical/central', 'X is widely adopted in mission-critical applications', 'X raises serious concerns', and count how many sentences pass before the first sentence describing what was actually done. 0 = the first sentence already states what was done; 5 = one framing sentence of stakes; 10 = three or more sentences of stakes, motivation and concern before any contribution appears. Score only the amount of importance-framing. Do NOT judge whether the stated importance is true, and do NOT judge whether framing the stakes is good writing.
selected.rationale: The stakes-first template sits on the card-high side: R13 opens 'Handling implicit language is essential...' (card .965), R56 'Efficient inference in high-dimensional models is a central challenge' (card .920), R34 'A critical component to enabling intelligent reasoning ... is memory' (card .813), R28 'critical to ensure their safety against adversarial attacks' (card .805), R30 'widely adopted in mission-critical applications' (card .786). The dense-favoured items instead open on the object itself: R26 'We study the cost of overfitting', R31 'We introduce the 2-simplicial Transformer', R42 'We seek to uncover'. Stakes language is a rehearsable opening move, so any bank criterion resembling 'is the problem motivated' can be satisfied by writing habit alone. Marked mixed because groups that teach the template may also mentor better research.
member_names: Importance preamble before any contribution is stated
